newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Petrol shortage hits oil-producing Nigeria.
newsitem.headline: Petrol shortage hits oil-producing Nigeria.

text.p: A two-week-old petrol shortage in Africa's leading oil-producing nation is worsening and a Nigerian government newspaper on Saturday dubbed it the "shame of a nation".
Mile-long queues of vehicles formed at the few stations still dispensing petrol in Lagos, Nigeria's biggest city and commercial hub.
"I queued before day break and I am not sure of getting any fuel," motorist Deola Adebambo said seven hours after beginning his wait.

Reports from other parts the country said the shortage had spread to much of southwestern Nigeria. Residents of the inland capital Abuja, where Nigeria's military rulers live, said petrol queues had begun to form in that city.

In Lagos, unemployed youths seized the opportunity to hawk fuel at four times the normal price. Thousands of commuters were stranded along major roads on Saturday while commercial buses and taxis have hiked fares.
Fuel shortages occur frequently in Nigeria and last a few days but the current crisis is showing no sign of easing.
"This is the second week, yet the problem has been going from bad to worse," said the government-owned Weekend Times newspaper in a front-page report headlined "Shame of a nation."
So far there has been no clear explanation from state-run Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC) nor its subsidiary the Pipelines and Products Marketing Company (PPMC) on the cause.
"PPMC is to blame for inefficiency," said the Times. Nigeria has four refineries able to process 445,000 barrels of crude oil daily but operates well below that.
Industry sources have blamed the shortage on damage at the key Port Harcourt refinery. NNPC denies this and its spokesman Edem Duke told state television early this week the scarcity would soon end.
When the shortage began NNPC blamed it on immigration officers delaying a vessel laden with petrol because the crew had no identity papers.
But the chief of immigration, Sahibi Dange told Weekend Times: "How can a brief apprehension of only three crew members of just one vessel have caused a lingering crisis?"
